title: Population vs. sample
meaning: The population is every member of the group you care about. A sample is the part of it you actually measure, because measuring everyone is usually too slow or costly.
Analysts care because almost every result they report comes from a sample, so they need to know how well it stands for the whole population.
rule: Population: everyone or everything in the group the question is about. Sample: the members you actually measure.
Parameter: a true value for the population, such as the real average. Statistic: the same value worked out from a sample, used as an estimate.
A random sample gives every member the same chance of selection, which keeps the estimate fair.

example.intro: A retailer has 5,000 customers and surveys 250 of them, chosen at random, about delivery speed.

table.caption: Population and sample terms for the delivery survey
head: Term
In this survey
rows: The true average rating of all 5,000 (unknown)
The average rating of the 250 (what we report)

steps: Sample share = 250 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 5% of the customers.
The statistic (the sample average) is our estimate of the parameter (the population average).
Choosing at random means every customer had the same chance of being picked, so the sample is less likely to be biased.

trap.wrong: Calling the sample result a parameter, or assuming a sample tells you about a group it was not drawn from.
trap.why: A parameter belongs to the population and a statistic to the sample: "s" for sample, "p" for population is an easy way to remember it. A survey of web visitors says little about customers who only shop in store.

title: Null and alternative hypotheses
meaning: A hypothesis test starts with two opposite statements: the null hypothesis, which says nothing has changed, and the alternative, which is the claim you want evidence for.
Analysts care because the exam often gives a scenario and asks which pair of hypotheses fits it.
rule: H₀, the null hypothesis: no change or no difference. It always uses the equals sign, for example mean = $8,000.
H₁, the alternative hypothesis: the claim being tested. It uses > (greater), < (less) or ≠ (not equal), copied from the scenario.
One-tailed test: H₁ uses > or <, one direction only. Two-tailed test: H₁ uses ≠, either direction.
The test then asks whether the data give enough evidence to reject H₀ in favour of H₁.

example.intro: A manager says mean weekly sales are now greater than $8,000. Write the hypotheses.
steps: The claim is "greater than $8,000", so that is H₁: mean > $8,000.
H₀ is the no-change position with the equals sign: mean = $8,000.
The claim names one direction (greater), so this is a one-tailed test.
If the claim were "sales have changed", H₁ would be mean ≠ $8,000, a two-tailed test.

trap.wrong: Putting the claim in H₀, or using the wrong direction in H₁.
trap.why: H₀ always holds the equals sign and the "no effect" position; the claim goes in H₁. Copy the direction from the wording: "more than" gives >, "less than" gives <, "different" or "changed" gives ≠.

title: Type I and Type II errors
meaning: A hypothesis test can be wrong in two ways: it can find an effect that is not there (Type I), or miss one that is (Type II).
Analysts care because the two mistakes have different costs, and the exam asks which one a scenario describes.
rule: Type I error (false positive): rejecting H₀ when it is true. Its chance is α, the significance level.
Type II error (false negative): failing to reject H₀ when it is false.
α, the Greek letter alpha, is the Type I risk the analyst chooses before testing, usually 0.05 (5%).

example.intro: A spam filter tests each email. H₀: "this email is genuine." H₁: "this email is spam."

table.caption: The four outcomes of the spam filter
head: Filter decision
Email is genuine (H₀ true)
Email is spam (H₀ false)
rows: Lets it through (fail to reject H₀)

steps: A genuine email sent to the spam folder is a Type I error.
A spam email that reaches the inbox is a Type II error.
Lowering α (say from 0.05 to 0.01) makes Type I errors rarer but Type II errors more likely.

trap.wrong: Swapping the two: calling a missed effect a Type I error.
trap.why: Type I comes first, like a false alarm: it rejects a true H₀. Type II is a miss: it keeps a false H₀. Find what H₀ says in the scenario, then ask whether the decision rejected it wrongly or kept it wrongly.

title: p-values and significance
meaning: A p-value says how surprising the data would be if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value means the data would be unusual under H₀, which is evidence against it.
Analysts care because "statistically significant" in a report means the p-value fell below the chosen significance level.
rule: The p-value: if H₀ were true, the chance of getting results at least as extreme as the ones observed.
α, the significance level, is the cut-off chosen before the test, usually 0.05.
If p ≤ α, reject H₀: the result is statistically significant. If p > α, fail to reject H₀.
The confidence level that matches α is (1 − α) × 100, so α = 0.05 goes with 95%.

example.intro: An A/B test of two email subject lines gives p = 0.03. The team chose α = 0.05 before the test.

table.caption: Decisions for three p-values at α = 0.05
head: p-value
Compared with 0.05
Decision
rows: Fail to reject H₀: not significant

steps: 0.03 ≤ 0.05, so reject H₀: the difference in open rates is statistically significant.
The confidence level that goes with α = 0.05 is (1 − 0.05) × 100 = 95%.
Significant does not mean large: a tiny difference can be significant in a huge sample.

trap.wrong: Reading the p-value as the chance that H₀ is true, or saying "accept H₀" when p is large.
trap.why: The p-value is worked out by assuming H₀ is true, so it cannot be the chance that H₀ is true. A large p-value only means there is not enough evidence against H₀: say "fail to reject H₀".

title: Confidence intervals
meaning: A confidence interval is a range around a sample result that is likely to contain the true population value, such as "average spend is $46, give or take $4".
Analysts care because a single number from a sample hides its uncertainty; the interval shows how precise the estimate is.

formula.spoken: the interval is the sample mean, x bar, plus or minus the margin of error

symbols.meaning: "x bar", the mean of the sample
plus or minus: subtract for the lower bound, add for the upper bound
how far the interval reaches each side of the mean; it is given on the exam, not computed

example.intro: A sample of orders has a mean of $46. The 95% confidence interval uses a margin of error of $4.
steps: Lower bound = 46 − 4 = $42.
Upper bound = 46 + 4 = $50.
The interval is $42 to $50, and its width is 50 − 42 = $8, twice the margin of error.
Read it as: "the method we used catches the true mean in about 95% of samples."
A larger sample gives a smaller margin of error, so a narrower interval.

trap.wrong: Saying there is a 95% chance the true mean is in this particular interval, or that 95% of the data lie in it.
trap.why: The 95% describes the method across many samples, not this one interval, which either contains the true mean or does not. And the interval is about the mean, not individual values: most single orders may fall outside it.

title: Choosing a test: t-test, chi-squared, ANOVA
meaning: Different questions need different tests. The exam does not ask you to compute them, only to name the one that fits a scenario.
Analysts care because the wrong test gives a wrong answer even when the arithmetic is perfect.
rule: t-test: compares the means of two groups (a number measured in each group).
ANOVA (Analysis of Variance): compares the means of three or more groups.
Chi-squared test (χ², said "kai squared"): checks whether two category variables are related, using counts.

example.intro: Match each question to a test.

table.caption: Scenarios and the test that fits
head: Question
Data
Test
rows: Does layout A or B have higher average spend?
Do four couriers differ in mean delivery time?
Is payment method related to region?

steps: Ask first: is the outcome a number (spend, time) or a category (card, cash)?
For a number, count the groups: two means a t-test, three or more means ANOVA.
For categories, use chi-squared.

trap.wrong: Running several t-tests to compare three or more groups.
trap.why: Each extra t-test adds another chance of a false positive. ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) compares all the group means in one test.
